question.text: Will a federal grand jury in Washington, D.C. have returned and publicly disclosed an indictment against James Comey over his 2016 disclosure to The New York Times by November 13, 2026?
question.resolution_criteria: This question resolves on the status of United States v. Comey, No. 1:26-cr-00229 (TNM) (D.D.C.) as of 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026. It resolves YES if, by that time, a federal grand jury sitting in the District of Columbia has returned an indictment (including a superseding indictment) charging James Brien Comey, Jr. with the October 2016 disclosure conduct alleged in the criminal information in that case — including any charge that rests on that disclosure as an element or as part of a broader scheme or conspiracy — and the return of that indictment has been publicly disclosed. It resolves NO if no such indictment has been returned and publicly disclosed by that time, including if the criminal information has been dismissed without any indictment being returned, or if a grand jury has declined to indict. Resolution will be based on [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) reporting the return of such an indictment; the authoritative record of the case is its public docket.
question.fine_print: An indictment filed under a different District of Columbia criminal case number counts if it charges the same October 2016 disclosure conduct; an indictment charging only unrelated conduct (for example, conduct from 2017 or later) does not. An indictment that has been returned but remains sealed and undisclosed as of 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026 does not count.

research:

## 1. Resolution source
- The authoritative record is the public docket for US v. Comey, No. 1:26-cr-00229 (TNM). I couldn't read it: CourtListener's docket pages blocked me (HTTP 403). So I can't report its latest entry directly.
- 2026-10-26: Judge McFadden unsealed the case. The only charging document then was the two-count criminal information (§ 793(d) and conspiracy under §§ 793(d) and (g)). [memorandum order](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.297297/gov.uscourts.dcd.297297.14.0.pdf)

## 2. Current status
- No indictment has been returned or disclosed, as far as I could find. Searches for a November 2026 indictment in this case found nothing ([ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/grand-jury-indicts-former-fbi-director-james-comey/story?id=132425678), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecution_of_James_Comey)). Nothing settles the question yet.
- 2026-10-30: The latest reports still describe the government as "going to the grand jury very diligently." The prosecutor said grand jurors "may indict, they may not indict." [Spokesman-Review](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/oct/30/doj-seeks-grand-jury-indictment-of-comey-on-defens/), [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-30/doj-seeks-grand-jury-indictment-of-comey-in-defense-secrets-case)

## 3. Recent news (newest first)

- About 2026-10-30 to 11-02: A D.C. grand jury refused to indict in a 2024 double-voting case, according to the NYT as relayed by [Political Wire](https://politicalwire.com/2026/11/02/grand-jury-refuses-to-indict-in-voter-fraud-case/). The pieces give the date inconsistently: "Friday, November 02" and "Friday, November 6," but Friday was October 30. Raw Story's write-up is [here](https://www.rawstory.com/trump-doj-2678192314/).

  - floated waiting to see whether DOJ gets an indictment, which would make the limitations question moot if none comes;
  - remarked that "Grand juries do surprising things," and warned against a "dawn raid."

  The prosecutor said a grand jury might find the conspiracy ran as late as April 2017, which would keep the 10-year window open for that charge. [Yahoo](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/judge-mulls-throwing-doj-leak-192425252.html), [NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/james-comey-team-court-seeking-toss-third-doj-case-longtime-trump-foe-rcna606394), [Washington Times](https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2026/oct/30/judge-delays-decision-comey-case-justice-department-seeks-new/)

[DOJ](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/federal-grand-jury-indicts-former-fbi-director-james-comey-threats-harm-president-trump)

## 4. Base rates
- Historically, grand juries almost never decline to indict ("no true bills" are extremely rare, per NYT coverage). D.C. grand juries in 2025-26, however, have repeatedly refused in politically charged cases: Hutchinson on October 27, the voter-fraud case in late October, and others the reporting mentions.
- In Comey's own 2025 Virginia case, the grand jury indicted on two counts but declined a third. [Turley](https://jonathanturley.org/2025/09/26/martyr-or-liar-comey-indicted-on-two-counts/)
- I found no systematic data on D.C. no-bill rates for 2026.

forecasts.reasoning:
**(a) Time left and what Yes requires.** About 10 days remain (to 23:59 UTC, November 13, 2026). Yes requires a D.C. federal grand jury to return an indictment charging Comey with the October 2016 disclosure, either directly or as part of a conspiracy running through April 2017. The return must also be publicly disclosed, for example on the docket or through credible reporting. The key date is around November 5, the reported Speedy Trial Act deadline.

**(b) Status quo.** No indictment exists. The case rests only on a criminal information, and the grand jury has not acted. If nothing changes, the question resolves No.

**(c) Base rate.** Historically, grand juries return no-bills in well under 1% of federal cases. So when DOJ seriously seeks an indictment, it usually gets one, which would imply a Yes rate above 90%. The relevant reference class is narrower: politically charged cases by this DOJ before D.C. grand juries in 2025-26. In that class, refusals have been frequent. My rough estimate is that indictments came perhaps 50-60% of the time. Timing adds a further discount.

**(d) Strongest evidence.**
- **For Yes:**
  - DOJ said on October 30 it is "going to the grand jury very diligently" and is working on an indictment.
  - A grand jury has been hearing evidence since about late August (the Richman subpoena, August 31).
  - The Kalshi market gives only 23% that the D.D.C. case is dismissed before January 1. That suggests traders expect the case to survive, most plausibly through an indictment.
  - A Virginia grand jury did indict Comey in 2025.
- **For No:**
  - DOJ filed an information on the last day of the limitations period instead of an indictment. That suggests it could not, or dared not, get a grand jury vote in time, despite having a grand jury since August.
  - A D.C. grand jury declined to indict Cassidy Hutchinson on October 27, and another D.C. grand jury refused in the voter-fraud case in late October.
  - On November 2, a D.C. magistrate dismissed a related case as "weaponization."
  - The prosecutor himself said grand jurors "may indict, they may not indict."
  - McFadden noted that "Grand juries do surprising things."

**(e) Scenarios.**
- **No:** The grand jury hears the presentation in the first week of November and declines, or DOJ delays. The information is then dismissed or left pending, with no indictment disclosed by November 13.
- **Yes:** On or before November 5, the grand jury returns a conspiracy indictment covering October 2016 through April 2017. It is filed publicly in No. 1:26-cr-00229 and widely reported.

**(f) Moving to a final number.** I start around 55%, reflecting DOJ's active effort tempered by the D.C. political-case refusal rate. I move down about 15 points for three reasons:
- The tell from filing an information instead of an indictment by October 5.
- The recent cluster of D.C. no-bills and judicial hostility.
- The short window and the requirement that the indictment be publicly disclosed.

The Kalshi dismissal market partly offsets this. However, it does not measure the same event, and its low dismissal probability could also reflect judicial delay.

Probability: 40%

That can be as a standalone count or as part of a conspiracy running into 2017, under this case number or a new D.C. one. The return must also be publicly disclosed by that time. The reported practical deadline is November 5, the possible Speedy Trial Act cutoff.

(b) If nothing changes, the outcome is No. As of November 3 there is no reported indictment, only the criminal information.

(c) Base rate: historically, grand juries return indictments in more than 99% of cases DOJ presents. That rate does not fit here. A better reference class is D.C. grand juries in 2025-26 politically charged cases brought by this DOJ, where several refusals have been reported:
- Hutchinson, October 27
- a voter-fraud case, around October 30
- multiple 2025 cases

In those cases DOJ obtained indictments perhaps 50-65% of the time, sometimes only after re-presenting. In Comey's 2025 Virginia case, the grand jury indicted on two of three counts. That gives a starting point of about 55%.

(d) Evidence:
- **For Yes:** On October 30 DOJ told the court it is "going to the grand jury very diligently" and may add a conspiracy theory running through April 2017. A grand jury has been active in the probe since roughly August 31, when it subpoenaed Richman. DOJ has strong institutional motivation to get this indictment. The Kalshi market gives only 23% that the D.D.C. case is dismissed before 2027, which implies the market expects the case to survive, plausibly through an indictment.
